# Draft:Medieval bookbinding furnishings

Furnishings in bookbinding are the functional pieces of metal that are used for a variety of purposes within medieval books. Furniture can refer to anything that is attached to the cover, through the book board. Types of furniture include, corner pieces (with raised boss’s), fastening (including strap or pin, and hooked closures), finestra (or title window), centerpiece, chain attachments, and binding strips. Each pieces was carefully developed and had a desired function, and became increasingly decorative These furnishings started out being cast metal, and slowly transitioned to using pounded metal sheets. Copper and brass were the most prominent metals used, for furnishings, but stronger metals such as iron and tin were used for the rivets, while luxury examples could be made from silver. Once created furnishings could have been used on several different manuscripts, as the cycle of reuse and rebinding was common with liturgical works. Metal furniture was used on a variety of objects, because of this they are normally classified as insignificant metal objects during archeological digs, making attributions and purpose even harder to discover. Most of the research on furniture is directed towards dating styles, and not on discovery of function, or importance of use. While bookbinding furniture may be used to identify style, and even the culture that created it, it is important to look at the binding as a whole when attempting to date or otherwise localizing the manuscripts. Book furnishings could be specialized by the patron, with libraries receiving the same for all of their editions, and wealthy patrons personalizing their silver furnishings with their families symbols or letters.
Some decorative techniques for book furnishings include: engraved lines, boarders, scale patterns and other simple motifs, more intricate designs do exist, but surviving examples are rare. Punched or drilled holes, for both decorative and functional purposes. Stamped complex designs, quatrefoils, dots, or dotted boarders, and monograms of initials have been discovered. Casted elements with animal motifs, and complex shapes for designs most commonly found in fastenings. Decorative nails heads are also sometimes used, their designs could range from simple and domed, to intricately carved shapes.
Decoration could also be achieved through additive materials. Gilding, could be added to furnishings to up the luxurious quality of a codex, or enameling could be used in conjunction with engraving to create colorful patterns.
Types of Book Furnishings
Fastenings:
Fastenings are attached to most parchment or vellum manuscripts.They were used to create compression between the book boards and the pages. Parchment being derived from animal skins, would swell with changes in humidity, and warp when not compressed. Fastenings solved the issue of the parchment warping. There are two common closure styles, hooked, and what is known as “strap and pin.”
Hooked closure, were created with a hooked piece of metal attached to the book board on one side, while a catch plate with a hole for the hook was attached, often with a hinge.The catch plate was a common source for artistic decoration, and included many of the popular motifs, simpler designs like lines, and boarders were engraved, while more intricate designs were punched onto the sheet metal. Embossing, drilling holes, and adding gold leaf were also popular additions. The catch plate could come in many different shapes, from triangular and square, to what is described as fish tail shaped.
Strap and pin closures were created with a leather strap with several rivets attached to the book board, and a hinge plate with a loop for the strap to go through. While simpler in construction, design elements were still developed for strap and pin closures, this included stylized loops of cast metal, gold leaf additions, and engraving and punching techniques on the hinged plate. There were several types of this closure, including a more belt like fastening known as double rectangular, or the simple closure of using a folded piece of metal to hold onto the leather.
Boss:
The boss is a raised domed area, the boss’s served an important purpose of stopping the heavy book covers from being damaged as they were opened, and protecting the precious cover material from becoming dirty. Boss’s could be created with cast or sheet metal The first examples are round with three nails holes, but quickly transitioned into a decorative style. The nail holes themselves would become highly decorative, as examples of decorative nail heads have been discovered Square, triangular, and tabbed designs existed, with square designs sometimes being tilted to a diamond shape.
Corner Piece:
The corner pieces protect book corners by reenforcing them from being damaged Corner pieces along with centerpieces typically had decorative elements and could have boss’s in the center. Corner pieces were made with sheet or cast metal, and could be highly decorative and stylistic, with punching, engraving or gilding, and in some cases they were even made of precious metals. Corner pieces were attached through several methods, including but not limited to, riveting, nails, and tabs. The holes for attachment begin simplistic, but quickly develop an important role in stylistic elements of the corner piece as decorative nails were sometimes used. Trefoil was a very commonly used design. Corner pieces could also be used as, a wrap around the corner edge of the book board, instead of being affixed to the front of the cover, these were less decorative however.
Another type of corner piece was edge guards and shoes. These pieces were added to protect the manuscript when being stored upright. Shoes could have studs attached to them, lifting the bottom edge of the manuscript up from the surface it was placed on to protect the valuable cover material.
Binding Strips:
Binding strips are protective against friction, and are put on the fore edge of the manuscript, these could be decorative. Binding strips are difficult to identify when detached from the manuscript, so few examples are known or survive.
Fenestra:
The Finestra also known as the title window are present in some later medieval bindings. These title windows are created by attaching a piece of parchment under a metal frame that is riveted to the book board. This metal frame creates the illusion of seeing through the book board to the text inside, and was sometimes accented with clear horn would be used to protect the piece of parchment. The use of the fenestra is to show the reader what was inside the codex and could be found on the front or the back of the manuscript depending on what country you were in. Early manuscripts did not include modern functions, like title pages, tables of contents, or publishing details, so the fenestra were an easy way to know what codex you were picking up before opening it, and was an important part in the development of the chain library system.
Centerpieces:
Centerpieces are decorative markers of the center of the book board. They could be interesting shapes, such as ovals, diamonds, and flower shapes. Centerpieces can also have a boss, and be ornamented with gilding, punching, and engraving. Centerpieces could denote the manuscript, be used as an extra boss, or as just a decorative element in a lavish manuscript.
Chain Attachment and Chains:
Some manuscripts show signs of having chains plates to attach the book chain used in the medieval library system. These chain plates were typically in the top center of the book, riveted to the book board. The chain would then be attached to a loop on the plate. The chains would keep the manuscript tethered to a certain radius, stopping theft. Chain links were often created using casting, while chain plates were made from sheet metal.
Difficulty in Identification:
Book furnishings are often misattributed in archeological digs. Some identifications are the wrong book furnishing type, others are attributed as miscellaneous metal objects. Once the metal furnishing has been removed from the cover, it becomes difficult to reattribute back to the same codex. When detached from the codex, it is difficult to know if the metal furnishing is for codex’s, clothing, decorations, or boxes, a form where boss’s also developed. Reexamination of previous archeological discoveries could lead to more information. Book furnishings have been discarded sometimes by the institutions that keep them, before modern conservation. During the decline of chain libraries, storage concerns lead to furnishings being removed, thus losing several examples.
Problems with Chronology:
Dating of book furnishings is difficult like dating the books themselves. Book furnishings may be dated much later than the books publication date. This is likely do to lead times in binding and the process. Dating the codex itself based on design of the book furnishings is also dubious, as the furnishings would often be reused and recycled. However, closure designs did change over time, allowing for chronology to be created, even if exact year is unknown Dating is also difficult because of the small sample size of surviving examples, when an older than expected discovery is made, it has to be noted that the discovery is the known first.
